covers.quote: Avoid using them in general content where possible.
Avoid using abbreviations in any public-facing content.
Abbreviations are useful in very limited circumstances:
in a table or chart, where space is unavailable for the full form of the word
when using ‘cont’ to show continuing text in another part of content (for example, on another page of a print newsletter) – the full form of the word is more helpful where space allows.
Semi-formal and informal content uses abbreviations more often.

examples.note: Uses the full word rather than an abbreviation.

examples.note: Uses an avoidable abbreviation in general correspondence.

rules.specification: Judge avoidability using the intended audience, available space and stated exceptions. The page gives no numerical limit on abbreviation frequency. Public-facing content is expressly discouraged from using abbreviations.
rules.violation_condition: An avoidable abbreviation appears in general or public-facing content rather than its full form, outside the limited uses the page allows.
when: Applies to general content where using the full word is possible, and to public-facing content.
Abbreviations are permitted in tables or charts where there is insufficient space for the full word; the full-form note is checked separately.
‘cont’ may mark text continuing elsewhere, but the full word is preferred where space allows.
The page recognises more frequent abbreviation use in semi-formal and informal content; the audience-understanding requirement still applies.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3 consolidate the limited-use contexts and exceptions; G-4 consolidates the general-content and public-facing restatements.

rules.quote: provide a note under the table or chart giving the full form
rules.violation_condition: A table or chart uses an abbreviation because space is insufficient for the full word, but has no note beneath it giving that abbreviation’s full form.
when: Applies when an abbreviation is used in a table or chart because there is insufficient space for the full word.
rules.why: This requires a specific textual note beneath a table or chart, distinct from avoiding abbreviations or defining them at first use.

covers.quote: Use abbreviations only if users will understand what they mean.

rules.quote: If there’s any doubt, define the abbreviation on first use.
rules.specification: Assess possible unfamiliarity relative to the intended audience. The page does not specify a familiarity threshold or a particular definition format.
rules.violation_condition: An abbreviation whose meaning may be unfamiliar to the intended users appears without a definition at its first use.
when: Applies when there is doubt that users will understand an abbreviation.
rules.why: G-2 combines the audience-understanding condition with its first-use definition requirement rather than producing two findings for the same unfamiliar abbreviation.

rules.quote: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on.
rules.specification: Interpret ‘unusual’ relative to the intended audience. An explanation makes otherwise unusual wording acceptable; the page gives no required explanation location or familiarity threshold.
rules.violation_condition: An unusual word, phrase or idiom is used without an explanation of its meaning.
when: Applies to unusual wording, including phrases and idioms.
Explained unusual wording is permitted.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3 treat explanation as an alternative to avoidance; this accessibility instruction extends beyond abbreviations.

rules.quote: Don’t put a full stop after most abbreviations
rules.violation_condition: An abbreviation is followed by a full stop outside the listed sentence-ending, scientific-name and ‘n.d.’ exceptions.

‘n.d.’ meaning ‘no date’ for the year of publication in references is an exception.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3 keep the full-stop exceptions within one check; G-4 absorbs the body restatement.
